Summer tanagers (Piranga rubra) exhibit a predictable sequence of early developmental events that is tightly coupled to thermal conditions during incubation. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after twelve days [ab = twelve days], a duration that aligns well with incubation periods reported for other North American members of the cardinalid family. Upon emergence, the altricial nestlings are notably small, with an initial wet weight recorded at 3.5 grams [Ww0 = 3.5 grams]. This modest hatchling mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available at the time of hatching and necessitates immediate and intensive parental provisioning. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately after the chick has dried, averages 4.2 grams [Wwb = 4.2 grams], a value that represents the first measurable body mass after the absorption of residual amniotic fluid. These early life-history traits, determined under controlled laboratory conditions using a representative clutch from a wild population in Arkansas, underscore the vulnerability of the neonate during the first few days of post-hatching life.

The nestling period of the Summer tanager proceeds rapidly under the warm conditions characteristic of its active season. When ambient temperatures average 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value near the upper end of the species' thermal neutral zone during the breeding months, a clear sequence of developmental milestones is observed. Fledging, defined as the age at which the young bird achieves sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at nine days after hatching [tx = nine days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This brief nestling stage is typical of open-cup nesting passerines vulnerable to predation. In a comparative context, this fledging age is somewhat shorter than that reported for the closely related Scarlet tanager, which may reflect differences in nest-site concealment and parental defense strategies. Supporting these rapid developmental rates is a correspondingly early attainment of sexual maturity, with puberty estimated at 27 days after hatching [tp = 27 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. It should be noted that gonadal maturation and behavioral breeding readiness do not coincide, as first reproductive effort is deferred considerably.

Breeding phenology in the Summer tanager is characterized by a single productive reproductive event each year rather than by high clutch frequency. Under thermal regimes averaging 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], meaning that first-year birds typically do not breed until the summer following their hatching year. This deferred breeding contrasts with the rapid sexual maturation and suggests a life-history strategy in which young birds prioritize foraging experience and territory acquisition over early reproduction. Clutch size ranges from three to five eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = three to five eggs per nesting attempt], a moderate fecundity for a bird of this body size. Females produce only a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year], a reproductive frequency that is constrained by the extended incubation and dependent nestling phases, as well as the energetic demands of molting prior to fall migration.

Adult body mass in the Summer tanager shows modest sexual dimorphism, consistent with patterns observed across the genus Piranga. The ultimate wet weight for males, representing the maximum body mass attained by fully mature individuals, averages 29.1 grams [Wwi = 29.1 grams]. This male-biased mass is slightly lower than the species-level asymptotic adult mass of 29.5 grams [Wwi = 29.5 grams], a value derived from field measurements of both sexes combined. The difference, though small, may reflect differential investment in flight muscle and fat storage prior to migration, with males arriving on the breeding grounds earlier and in leaner condition than females. When considered in relation to the initial hatchling mass of 3.5 grams [Ww0 = 3.5 grams], the adult mass represents a roughly eight-fold increase in wet weight, a growth factor that is accomplished within a brief period of intense parental provisioning. These mass data were collected during a long-term banding study in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley.

Longevity records for the Summer tanager indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.9 years [am = approximately 7.9 years] when measured under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic range at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lifespan is modest relative to other cardinalids of comparable body size, such as the Northern cardinal, which may live considerably longer in the wild. The comparatively short lifespan suggests elevated annual mortality rates, likely attributable to the hazards of long-distance migration between breeding grounds in the southeastern United States and wintering areas in Central and South America. With a single clutch produced per year [F_R_i = a single clutch produced per year], containing 3 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = containing 3 to 5 eggs], the species' lifetime reproductive output is constrained by both fecundity per event and event frequency. In contrast to the extended development seen in some tropical resident passerines, the brief interval of about nine days after hatching [tx = about nine days after hatching] that characterizes the fledging period of this species underscores the high-risk, high-gain developmental strategy typical of open-nesting Neotropical migra at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]nts.
